definition: Attribution means the act of assigning a cause, source, or credit to someone or something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word attribution. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know attribution should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The museum revised its attribution of the unsigned portrait after pigment tests pointed to a different painter's workshop.
Speculation merely guesses at where something came from, while an attribution formally assigns it to a source or cause.
An attribution assigns responsibility based on evidence, but a verdict makes that assignment official and binding.

Ascription means assigning a quality, work, or motive to someone, and it is the rarer, more formal cousin. Attribution is the standard working word in art, journalism, and science for pinning a work or an effect to its source. You might read of the ascription of motives to a rival, but museums and newsrooms deal in attribution.

Crediting means naming someone as responsible for something good — a discovery, a song, an idea. Attribution is wider: it assigns credit, blame, or cause alike, and it can be tentative or disputed. You credit a songwriter; a lab report offers an attribution of an outbreak to a contaminated well.

After a record flood, reporters wanted to know whether a warming climate was to blame.

A research team simulated the same storm in model worlds with and without warmer oceans, then published a careful attribution of the disaster, assigning about a third of the extra rainfall to the warming and the rest to an unlucky alignment of weather patterns.
Their task was not to praise or accuse anyone, but to assign the right share of the outcome to the right cause.
The scientists formally assigned shares of the flood to specific causes, and that act of assigning is exactly what attribution means.
formal, academic/journalistic register
Attribution takes 'of' for the thing assigned and 'to' for its source (the attribution of the quote to Twain).
It covers credit, blame, and cause alike: scientists speak of the attribution of a heat wave to a warming climate just as editors speak of the attribution of a quotation to its speaker.

Three days after the ridge fire was contained, two rumors competed in town: a downed power line, or a campfire left by hikers.
The investigators refused to hurry, walking the burn scar backward toward its origin while the rumors grew louder.
Their final report's attribution surprised everyone: the fire began at neither, but at a lightning-struck snag that had smoldered unseen for a week.
The report laid out its evidence plainly -- char patterns, a scarred stump, weather logs from the night of the storm.
The power company, braced for lawsuits, published the finding in full; assigning the fire to lightning had settled in one page what weeks of rumor never could.
